records.source: וַיֵּ֖דַע יוֹאָ֣ב בֶּן־צְרֻיָ֑ה כִּֽי־לֵ֥ב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ עַל־אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And knew Joab son of Zeruiah that [the] heart of the king [was] on Absalom.
pieces: Joab son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart was set on Absalom.

L.1: And Joab son of Zeruiah knew that the heart of the king [was] on Absalom.

R.1: Joab, the son of Zeruiah, could tell that the king's heart was turning toward Absalom.

decisions.choice: the king's heart was on Absalom: his thoughts and longing were turned toward him
alternatives: the king's heart was against Absalom
decisions.reason: The phrase says only that the king's heart was "on" Absalom. Coming after 13:39, where David's grief for Amnon eases and he longs to go out to Absalom, it is taken as longing: Joab sees that David wants his son back but will not act. The same words can mean that the heart is set against someone, and David's refusal to see Absalom in verse 24 shows that his feelings were mixed. The verse does not settle how much was love and how much was anger.

decisions.choice: Joab son of Zeruiah: David's nephew and army commander
decisions.reason: Zeruiah was David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), and her son Joab commanded David's army (8:16). He is the one who now works to bring Absalom home.

decisions.choice: was set on (Balanced); was turning toward (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the open phrase "set on". Readable says plainly that his heart was moving toward Absalom, following meaning decision m1.

records.heading: Joab and the woman from Tekoa

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יוֹאָב֙ תְּק֔וֹעָה וַיִּקַּ֥ח מִשָּׁ֖ם אִשָּׁ֣ה חֲכָמָ֑ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵ֠לֶיהָ הִֽתְאַבְּלִי־נָ֞א וְלִבְשִׁי־נָ֣א בִגְדֵי־אֵ֗בֶל וְאַל־תָּס֨וּכִי֙ שֶׁ֔מֶן וְהָיִ֕ית כְּאִשָּׁ֗ה זֶ֚ה יָמִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים מִתְאַבֶּ֖לֶת עַל־מֵֽת׃
records.gloss: And sent Joab to Tekoa and took from there a woman wise, and said to her, Play the mourner please, and put on please garments of mourning, and not anoint [yourself with] oil, and be like a woman this many days mourning over [the] dead.
pieces: So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, "Act as though you are in mourning. Put on mourning clothes and do not anoint yourself with oil. Behave like a woman who has been grieving for the dead a long time.

L.2: And Joab sent to Tekoa and took a wise woman from there, and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner, please, and put on garments of mourning, and do not anoint yourself [with] oil, and be like a woman [who has been] mourning these many days for the dead.

R.2: So Joab sent for a wise woman from the town of Tekoa. He told her, "Pretend that someone in your family has died. Wear the clothes people wear when they are grieving. Do not put oil on your skin and hair to look nice. Act like a woman who has been sad over a death for a long time.

decisions.choice: a wise woman: a woman known for her skill with words and counsel
decisions.reason: "Wise" here means more than clever. Some women were known in their towns for sound counsel and persuasive speech; another wise woman saves the town of Abel in 20:16-22. Joab chooses her because she can carry off the part and argue her case before the king.

decisions.choice: Tekoa: a town in the hill country of Judah
decisions.reason: Tekoa lay about ten miles south of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness. It was later the home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1).

decisions.choice: do not anoint yourself with oil: leave off the usual grooming of someone not in mourning
decisions.reason: Rubbing olive oil on the skin and hair was part of everyday care and of looking well. Mourners left it off, as David did while his child was sick and took it up again afterward (12:20). A woman without it, in mourning clothes, would look as though her grief were old and deep.

decisions.choice: sent for; Pretend that someone in your family has died; to look nice
decisions.reason: Readable says that Joab sent for the woman rather than went himself, explains what playing the mourner means, and says why oil was used.

records.source: וּבָאת֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְדִבַּ֥רְתְּ אֵלָ֖יו כַּדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיָּ֧שֶׂם יוֹאָ֛ב אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים בְּפִֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And go to the king and speak to him according to the word the this. And put Joab the words in her mouth.
pieces: Then go to the king and speak to him in this way." And Joab put the words in her mouth.

L.3: And go to the king and speak to him according to this word." And Joab put the words in her mouth.

R.3: Then go to the king and say this to him." And Joab told her exactly what to say.

decisions.choice: put the words in her mouth: told her what to say
decisions.reason: The phrase means to give someone the words to speak, as Moses was to put words in Aaron's mouth (Exodus 4:15). The plan is Joab's, but how she speaks is her own skill (verse 2).

decisions.choice: this word: the speech Joab gives her, which the story does not repeat
decisions.reason: The narrator does not report Joab's instructions. The reader hears them for the first time as the woman speaks to the king.

decisions.choice: told her exactly what to say
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture of putting words in her mouth means.

records.source: וַ֠תֹּאמֶר הָאִשָּׁ֤ה הַתְּקֹעִית֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַתִּפֹּ֧ל עַל־אַפֶּ֛יהָ אַ֖רְצָה וַתִּשְׁתָּ֑חוּ וַתֹּ֖אמֶר הוֹשִׁ֥עָה הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ס
records.gloss: And said the woman the Tekoite to the king, and she fell on her face to [the] ground and bowed down, and said, Save, O king!
pieces: When the woman of Tekoa addressed the king, she threw herself face down on the ground and bowed low. "Help me, Your Majesty!" she said.

L.4: And the Tekoite woman spoke to the king, and she fell on her face to the ground and bowed down, and said, "Save [me], O king!"

R.4: The woman from Tekoa went to speak to the king. She bowed down with her face to the ground and said, "Please help me, Your Majesty!"

decisions.choice: spoke to the king: following the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The Hebrew begins "And the woman said to the king", though her words come only at the end of the verse. Many Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient translations read "came to the king", which differs in one letter group and reads more smoothly. Either way the sense is that she came before the king to speak. This translation keeps the Hebrew text and takes it as the start of her approach.

decisions.choice: Save, O king: a plea for the king's help in a matter of justice
decisions.reason: Anyone could cry out to the king to step in when the ordinary courts could not help (compare 2 Kings 6:26). Falling face down and bowing low showed her humility before the king.

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "Your Majesty" for the address "O king", the way a king is addressed in English.

records.source: וַיֹּֽאמֶר־לָ֥הּ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מַה־לָּ֑ךְ וַתֹּ֗אמֶר אֲבָ֛ל אִשָּֽׁה־אַלְמָנָ֥ה אָ֖נִי וַיָּ֥מָת אִישִֽׁי׃
records.gloss: And said to her the king, What [is] to you? And she said, Truly, a woman widow [am] I, and died my husband.
pieces: The king asked her, "What is troubling you?" She answered, "Sadly, I am a widow. My husband is dead.

L.5: And the king said to her, "What [is the matter] with you?" And she said, "Truly, I [am] a widow woman, and my husband has died.

R.5: The king asked her, "What is wrong?" She answered, "I am a widow. My husband has died.

decisions.choice: what is to you: what is your trouble
decisions.reason: The question asks what has happened to the one who comes asking for help (Judges 18:23; 2 Kings 6:28).

decisions.choice: truly: a sad affirmation, "alas, it is so"
decisions.reason: The word affirms what follows with a note of grief. The repeated statement that she is a widow and that her husband is dead stresses that she has no man to protect her or carry on the family.

decisions.choice: Sadly
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "Sadly" for the sorrowful "truly"; Readable leaves it to the tone of the sentence.

records.source: וּלְשִׁפְחָֽתְךָ֙ שְׁנֵ֣י בָנִ֔ים וַיִּנָּצ֤וּ שְׁנֵיהֶם֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה וְאֵ֥ין מַצִּ֖יל בֵּֽינֵיהֶ֑ם וַיַּכּ֧וֹ הָאֶחָ֛ד אֶת־הָאֶחָ֖ד וַיָּ֥מֶת אֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And to your maidservant [were] two sons, and fought the two of them in the field, and [there was] no [one] separating between them, and struck the one the other and killed him.
pieces: Your servant had two sons. The two of them got into a fight out in the field, with no one there to pull them apart, and one struck the other and killed him.

L.6: And your maidservant had two sons, and the two of them fought in the field, and [there was] no one to separate them, and the one struck the other and killed him.

R.6: I had two sons. They began fighting out in the fields, and no one was there to stop them. One of them hit the other and killed him.

decisions.choice: two brothers fighting in the field: a story shaped like Cain and Abel and like Absalom and Amnon
decisions.reason: The fight in the field, with no one near, echoes Cain killing Abel in the field (Genesis 4:8). It also mirrors David's own family: Absalom had his brother Amnon killed (13:28-29). The woman tells a case that seems to be hers so that the king will judge it before he sees that it is about him (compare Nathan's story in 12:1-7).

decisions.choice: no one separating them: no one to pull them apart
decisions.reason: The word usually means one who rescues. Here it is someone who could have stepped in and stopped the fight. The point is that the killing was not planned, and that there were no witnesses.

decisions.choice: your maidservant: a humble way to speak of herself
decisions.reason: Shifchah is a servant girl of low rank. Speaking of herself as the king's servant is the polite form of a petitioner (1 Samuel 1:18; 25:24).

decisions.choice: your maidservant (Literal); your servant (Balanced); I (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Samuel 1 and 25, Literal keeps "maidservant", Balanced keeps the humble third person with "your servant", and Readable says "I" and "me" through the woman's speech.

records.source: וְהִנֵּה֩ קָ֨מָה כָֽל־הַמִּשְׁפָּחָ֜ה עַל־שִׁפְחָתֶ֗ךָ וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ תְּנִ֣י׀אֶת־מַכֵּ֣ה אָחִ֗יו וּנְמִתֵ֨הוּ֙ בְּנֶ֤פֶשׁ אָחִיו֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָרָ֔ג וְנַשְׁמִ֖ידָה גַּ֣ם אֶת־הַיּוֹרֵ֑שׁ וְכִבּ֗וּ אֶת־גַּֽחַלְתִּי֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁאָ֔רָה לְבִלְתִּ֧י שִׂים־לְאִישִׁ֛י שֵׁ֥ם וּשְׁאֵרִ֖ית עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָאֲדָמָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And look, has risen all the clan against your maidservant, and they say, Give [up] the [one] striking his brother, and we will put him to death for [the] life of his brother whom he killed, and we will destroy also the heir. And they will quench my coal which is left, so as not to set for my husband a name and a remnant on [the] face of the ground.
pieces: Now the whole clan has risen up against your servant. They say, 'Hand over the man who struck down his brother. We will put him to death to pay for the life of the brother he killed, and so do away with the heir as well.' So they would put out the one coal I have left, and leave my husband neither name nor survivor on the face of the earth."

L.7: And now the whole clan has risen against your maidservant, and they say, 'Give up the one who struck his brother, and we will put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed, and we will destroy the heir also.' And they will quench my coal that is left, so as not to leave for my husband a name or a remnant on the face of the ground."

R.7: Now the whole family has turned against me. They are saying, 'Hand over the one who killed his brother. We will put him to death to pay for his brother's life. That will get rid of the heir too.' My son is all I have left, like the last glowing coal of a fire. If they put him out, my husband will have no one left on earth to carry on his name."

decisions.choice: the clan claims his life for his brother's life
decisions.reason: The law gave the dead man's near relatives the duty of taking the life of a killer (Numbers 35:19). Here the family itself demands it, though the killer is one of their own and the only son left to his widowed mother.

decisions.choice: and we will destroy the heir also: the cost of their demand, put in their own mouths
decisions.reason: By having the relatives call him "the heir", the woman shows what they would take from her: the one who would carry on the family and its land. It may also hint that the land would pass to the relatives who are demanding his death.

decisions.choice: quench my coal that is left: put out her last hope for the family
decisions.reason: A live coal kept in the ashes could light the fire again. Her one surviving son is the last spark of her husband's line; killing him would put the family out for good.

decisions.choice: a name and a remnant: a descendant to carry on the family
decisions.reason: A man's name lived on through his sons (Deuteronomy 25:6; Numbers 27:4). Without a son, the dead man's family would vanish from the land.

decisions.choice: My son is all I have left, like the last glowing coal of a fire. If they put him out ...
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the coal and names the son, so that the reader sees what she means.

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶל־הָאִשָּׁ֖ה לְכִ֣י לְבֵיתֵ֑ךְ וַאֲנִ֖י אֲצַוֶּ֥ה עָלָֽיִךְ׃
records.gloss: And said the king to the woman, Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you.
pieces: The king said to the woman, "Go home. I will give orders about your case."

L.8: And the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."

R.8: The king told the woman, "Go home. I will give orders to take care of your problem."

decisions.choice: I will give orders concerning you: a promise to act, but without a firm ruling
decisions.reason: The king says he will deal with the matter but does not yet say how. The woman presses him for more in verses 9-11, until he binds himself by an oath.

decisions.choice: Go home
decisions.reason: "Go to your house" is said in English as "Go home".

records.source: וַתֹּ֜אמֶר הָאִשָּׁ֤ה הַתְּקוֹעִית֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עָלַ֞י אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ הֶעָוֺ֖ן וְעַל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑י וְהַמֶּ֥לֶךְ וְכִסְא֖וֹ נָקִֽי׃ס
records.gloss: And said the woman the Tekoite to the king, On me, my lord the king, [be] the guilt and on [the] house of my father; and the king and his throne [be] innocent.
pieces: The woman of Tekoa replied, "My lord the king, let the guilt be on me and on my father's house, and let the king and his throne be free of blame."

L.9: And the Tekoite woman said to the king, "On me, my lord the king, [be] the guilt, and on the house of my father; and the king and his throne [be] guiltless."

R.9: But the woman from Tekoa said, "Your Majesty, if anyone is to be blamed for this, let it be me and my father's family. Let no blame fall on you or on your throne."

decisions.choice: on me be the guilt: she takes on herself any guilt for sparing her son
decisions.reason: Letting a killer go free could leave blood guilt on the land (Numbers 35:31-33). She offers to carry any such guilt herself, with her family, so that the king may act without fear of it.

decisions.choice: the king and his throne: the king and his royal house
decisions.reason: The throne stands for the king's rule and the line of kings after him (7:16).

decisions.choice: my lord the king: the respectful way to address a king
decisions.reason: Speaking to the king in the third person, as "my lord the king", was the courtesy of the court (9:11).

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable puts the courtesy "my lord the king" as "Your Majesty" and speaks to the king as "you", as in 9:11.

records.source: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ הַֽמְדַבֵּ֤ר אֵלַ֨יִךְ֙ וַֽהֲבֵאת֣וֹ אֵלַ֔י וְלֹֽא־יֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד לָגַ֥עַת בָּֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And said the king, The [one] speaking to you, and you will bring him to me, and not he will again anymore touch you.
pieces: The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will never trouble you again."

L.10: And the king said, "The [one] who speaks to you, bring him to me, and he will not touch you again anymore."

R.10: The king said, "If anyone threatens you, bring him to me. He will never bother you again."

decisions.choice: touch you: harm or trouble you
decisions.reason: To touch someone often means to harm them (Genesis 26:11; Joshua 9:19). The king promises to protect her from anyone who presses the family's claim.

decisions.choice: the one speaking to you: anyone who speaks against you
decisions.reason: The phrase stands first for stress: whoever raises the matter with her is to be brought before the king.

decisions.choice: threatens you
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what kind of speaking the king means.

records.source: וַתֹּאמֶר֩ יִזְכָּר־נָ֨א הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֶת־יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ מֵהַרְבַּ֞ת גֹּאֵ֤ל הַדָּם֙ לְשַׁחֵ֔ת וְלֹ֥א יַשְׁמִ֖ידוּ אֶת־בְּנִ֑י וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ חַי־יְהוָ֔ה אִם־יִפֹּ֛ל מִשַּׂעֲרַ֥ת בְּנֵ֖ךְ אָֽרְצָה׃
records.gloss: And she said, Let remember please the king Yahweh your God, from [the] increasing of [the] avenger of the blood to destroy, and not they will destroy my son. And he said, [By the] life of Yahweh, not will fall from [the] hair of your son to [the] ground.
pieces: She said, "Please let the king call on {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, so that the avenger of blood will not add to the destruction, and my son will not be destroyed." He said, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not one hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."

L.11: And she said, "Please let the king remember {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, so that the avenger of blood does not increase the destroying, and they do not destroy my son." And he said, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not one of the hairs of your son shall fall to the ground."

R.11: Then she said, "Please, Your Majesty, make a promise in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. Then the relative who avenges the death will not be able to do more killing, and my son will not be destroyed." The king answered, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, not even one hair of your son's head will fall to the ground."

decisions.choice: let the king remember Yahweh: let him bind himself by an oath in Yahweh's name
decisions.reason: To "remember" Yahweh here is to call on his name. The woman wants more than an order; she wants the king's sworn word, which he gives at the end of the verse.

decisions.choice: the avenger of blood: the near relative bound to take the killer's life
decisions.reason: This is the go'el haddam of Numbers 35:19: the dead man's near relative, whose duty it was to put the killer to death. The woman asks the king to stop that duty from being carried out against her son.

decisions.choice: from the increasing of the avenger to destroy: so that he does not destroy still more
decisions.reason: The words say literally "from the avenger's making much of destroying". One son is already dead; the avenger would add a second death and wipe out the family.

decisions.choice: not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground: he will come to no harm at all
decisions.reason: The same oath protects Jonathan in 1 Samuel 14:45. The king now stands under an oath in Yahweh's name, which the woman will turn to Absalom.

decisions.choice: the relative who avenges the death
decisions.reason: Readable explains the avenger of blood as Numbers 35 does; Literal and Balanced keep "the avenger of blood".

decisions.choice: call on (Balanced); make a promise in the name of (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "remember" means here, following meaning decision m1.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה תְּדַבֶּר־נָ֧א שִׁפְחָתְךָ֛ אֶל־אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ דָּבָ֑ר וַיֹּ֖אמֶר דַּבֵּֽרִי׃ס
records.gloss: And said the woman, Let speak please your maidservant to my lord the king a word. And he said, Speak.
pieces: Then the woman said, "Please let your servant say one more thing to my lord the king." "Speak," he said.

L.12: And the woman said, "Please let your maidservant speak a word to my lord the king." And he said, "Speak."

R.12: Then the woman said, "Your Majesty, please let me say one more thing." "Go ahead," the king said.

decisions.choice: your maidservant: the woman's humble way of speaking of herself, as in verse 6
decisions.reason: She again speaks of herself as the king's servant and of him as "my lord the king", the courtesy of the court (verses 6 and 9). Having won her oath, she asks leave to go on.

decisions.choice: one more thing
decisions.reason: "A word" here is a further thing to say, after the king has already ruled; Balanced and Readable make that plain. Readable uses "me" and "Your Majesty" as in verses 6 and 9.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה וְלָ֧מָּה חָשַׁ֛בְתָּה כָּזֹ֖את עַל־עַ֣ם אֱלֹהִ֑ים וּמִדַּבֵּ֨ר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ הַדָּבָ֤ר הַזֶּה֙ כְּאָשֵׁ֔ם לְבִלְתִּ֛י הָשִׁ֥יב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶֽת־נִדְּחֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And said the woman, And why have you planned like this against [the] people of God? And from [the] speaking of the king the word the this [he is] like a guilty [one], in not bringing back the king his banished [one].
pieces: The woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? By speaking as he has, the king convicts himself, since the king has not brought home his own banished son.

L.13: And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing as this against the people of God? For in the king's speaking this word, [he is] like one guilty, in that the king has not brought back his banished one.

R.13: The woman said, "Then why have you planned something like this against God's people? By what you have just said, Your Majesty, you have shown that you yourself are in the wrong. You have not let your own son come back home from the place where he fled.

decisions.choice: planned such a thing against the people of God: kept Absalom from returning, to Israel's harm
decisions.reason: "Such a thing" is what the king has done in his own house: he has let his son stay away, as the clan would have done away with the widow's son. The people of God are Israel, who stand to lose the king's heir, just as her husband's line would be cut off (verse 7).

decisions.choice: in speaking this word the king is like one guilty: his own ruling condemns him
decisions.reason: By swearing to protect the widow's son, the king has judged a case like his own. If a killer may come home in her family, his ruling stands against his refusal to bring back Absalom (compare Nathan's "You are the man", 12:7).

decisions.choice: his banished one: Absalom, living in exile
decisions.reason: Absalom fled to Geshur after killing Amnon and stayed there three years (13:37-38). The word means one driven out or cast away; it returns in verse 14.

decisions.choice: Your Majesty, you
decisions.reason: The woman speaks of "the king" in the third person, as the court did. Readable says "you" so that it is plain she means David himself.

decisions.choice: his own banished son (Balanced); your own son (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Absalom as the king's son, which is what "his banished one" means here.

records.source: כִּי־מ֣וֹת נָמ֔וּת וְכַמַּ֨יִם֙ הַנִּגָּרִ֣ים אַ֔רְצָה אֲשֶׁ֖ר לֹ֣א יֵאָסֵ֑פוּ וְלֹֽא־יִשָּׂ֤א אֱלֹהִים֙ נֶ֔פֶשׁ וְחָשַׁב֙ מַֽחֲשָׁב֔וֹת לְבִלְתִּ֛י יִדַּ֥ח מִמֶּ֖נּוּ נִדָּֽח׃
records.gloss: For surely we will die, and like the water spilled on the ground which not will be gathered; and not takes away God life, and he devises plans so as not to be cast out from him [the] banished [one].
pieces: We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life; instead {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} devises ways for the banished one not to remain an outcast from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.14: For we will surely die, and [we are] like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up; and God does not take away life, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} devises plans so that the banished one is not cast out from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.14: All of us must die someday. We are like water spilled on the ground, which no one can gather up again. But God does not take life away. Instead, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} makes plans so that a person who has been sent away does not stay cut off from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: like water spilled on the ground: life, once gone, cannot be brought back
decisions.reason: Water poured out on dry ground soaks away and cannot be gathered again. The woman reminds the king that death is final: Amnon cannot be brought back, and if Absalom too is lost, nothing can undo it.

decisions.choice: God does not take away life, but devises plans: God's way is to restore, not to destroy
alternatives: God does not lift up a life (does not spare anyone from death)
God will not take away the life of one who devises plans to bring back the banished
decisions.reason: The words are short and hard to read. Taken as they stand, they say that God does not take away life but makes ways to bring back those who are banished; the king should do the same. Others read "God does not lift up a life", meaning God does not spare the dead from dying, as part of the picture of the spilled water. Others again change the text slightly to read "God will not take away the life of one who devises plans", that is, God will not punish the king for bringing his son back. The first reading follows the Hebrew without change and fits the woman's appeal.

decisions.choice: the banished one is not cast out from him: no one exiled remains shut out from God
decisions.reason: The word for "banished" is the one used of Absalom in verse 13. The pronoun refers to God, who does not leave the outcast cut off from himself. The same words can be read "from us", meaning from the community; the sense of bringing the exile home is the same.

decisions.choice: a person who has been sent away
decisions.reason: Readable says "sent away" for "banished", and keeps the general statement so that it applies to Absalom without naming him.

records.source: וְ֠עַתָּה אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֜אתִי לְדַבֵּ֨ר אֶל־הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲדֹנִי֙ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֥י יֵֽרְאֻ֖נִי הָעָ֑ם וַתֹּ֤אמֶר שִׁפְחָֽתְךָ֙ אֲדַבְּרָה־נָּ֣א אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אוּלַ֛י יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר אֲמָתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And now, that I have come to speak to the king my lord the word the this [is] because made me afraid the people; and said your maidservant, Let me speak please to the king; perhaps will do the king the word of his maidservant.
pieces: Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people frightened me. Your servant thought, 'Let me speak to the king. Perhaps the king will grant his servant's request.'

L.15: And now, [the reason] that I have come to speak this word to the king my lord [is] that the people made me afraid; and your maidservant said, 'Let me speak, please, to the king; perhaps the king will do the word of his maidservant.'

R.15: Your Majesty, I came to tell you all this because people were making me afraid. I thought, 'I will speak to the king. Maybe he will do what I ask.'

decisions.choice: the people made me afraid: she returns to her own case
decisions.reason: Having spoken of the king's son, she goes back to her story, so that the king will not feel cornered. "The people" may be her relatives who threaten her son (verse 7), or the people at large; in Joab's plan they may also stand for the nation that wants Absalom back.

decisions.choice: your maidservant said: she said to herself, thought
decisions.reason: To "say" here is to say to oneself, to think (Genesis 20:11).

decisions.choice: the word of his maidservant: her request
decisions.reason: She speaks of herself in the third person, as the king's servant, to the end of her plea (verses 6 and 12).

decisions.choice: thought
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "thought" for "said" where she speaks to herself.

decisions.choice: request
decisions.reason: Balanced says "request" for "word" where it means what she asks the king to do.

records.source: כִּ֚י יִשְׁמַ֣ע הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לְהַצִּ֥יל אֶת־אֲמָת֖וֹ מִכַּ֣ף הָאִ֑ישׁ לְהַשְׁמִ֨יד אֹתִ֤י וְאֶת־בְּנִי֙ יַ֔חַד מִֽנַּחֲלַ֖ת אֱלֹהִֽים׃
records.gloss: For will hear the king, to deliver his maidservant from [the] palm of the man [seeking] to destroy me and my son together from [the] inheritance of God.
pieces: For the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the one who seeks to destroy both me and my son, cutting us off from the inheritance God has given.

L.16: For the king will hear, to deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man [who would] destroy me and my son together from the inheritance of God.

R.16: I was sure that the king would listen and save me from the man who wants to destroy both me and my son. He would cut us off from the land God gave {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people.

decisions.choice: the inheritance of God: Israel's land and place among God's people
decisions.reason: The land was God's gift to Israel, shared out among its families as an inheritance (Numbers 26:52-56; 1 Samuel 26:19). To lose one's heir was to lose the family's share of it, and with it a place in God's people.

decisions.choice: the man who would destroy me and my son: the avenger who claims her son's life
decisions.reason: "The man" is the one pressing the clan's claim (verse 11). Killing her son would also destroy her, since she would be left without anyone to provide for her or carry on the family.

decisions.choice: the inheritance God has given (Balanced); the land God gave his people (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the inheritance of God is, following meaning decision m1. Readable adds "I was sure that" to join the verse to her thought in verse 15.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ שִׁפְחָ֣תְךָ֔ יִֽהְיֶה־נָּ֛א דְּבַר־אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לִמְנוּחָ֑ה כִּ֣י׀כְּמַלְאַ֣ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים כֵּ֣ן אֲדֹנִ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לִשְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ הַטּ֣וֹב וְהָרָ֔ע וַֽיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ יְהִ֥י עִמָּֽךְ׃פ
records.gloss: And said your maidservant, Let be please [the] word of my lord the king for rest; for like [the] angel of God, so [is] my lord the king to hear the good and the bad. And Yahweh your God be with you.
pieces: Your servant thought, 'Let what my lord the king says bring me rest, since my lord the king is like an angel of God in telling good from evil.' May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God be with you!"

L.17: And your maidservant said, 'Let the word of my lord the king be for rest, please; for like an angel of God, so [is] my lord the king to hear the good and the bad.' And may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God be with you!"

R.17: I thought, 'What the king says will give me peace. The king is like an angel from God. He knows what is good and what is evil.' May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God be with you!"

decisions.choice: like an angel of God: wholly good and wise
decisions.reason: To compare the king to an angel, a messenger from God, is high praise: he is wise and fair, and can be trusted to judge rightly. The same comparison is made of David by Achish (1 Samuel 29:9) and again by the woman in verse 20 and by Mephibosheth (19:28).

decisions.choice: to hear the good and the bad: to tell right from wrong in judging
decisions.reason: "Hear" here is to hear a case and judge it. Good and bad together mean the whole range of right and wrong (compare Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 3:9).

decisions.choice: for rest: a word that settles the matter and gives peace
decisions.reason: She hopes the king's ruling will end the threat to her son and give her rest. The same ruling will settle the matter of Absalom.

decisions.choice: an angel of God (Literal, Balanced); an angel from God (Readable)
decisions.reason: The phrase is a comparison with God's messengers in general, as in 1 Samuel 29:9, so it is worded as there: "an angel of God", and at Readable "an angel from God". "God" stands with the article in this verse, as often, without making it "the" angel.

records.source: וַיַּ֣עַן הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־הָ֣אִשָּׁ֔ה אַל־נָ֨א תְכַחֲדִ֤י מִמֶּ֨נִּי֙ דָּבָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י שֹׁאֵ֣ל אֹתָ֑ךְ וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה יְדַבֶּר־נָ֖א אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And answered the king and said to the woman, Do not please hide from me a word which I [am] asking you. And said the woman, Let speak please my lord the king.
pieces: Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I am about to ask you." "Let my lord the king speak," the woman said.

L.18: And the king answered and said to the woman, "Please do not hide from me anything that I am asking you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak, please."

R.18: Then the king answered her, "I have a question for you. Do not hide the truth from me." The woman said, "Ask me, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: do not hide from me anything that I ask: answer me fully and truthfully
decisions.reason: The king sees the purpose behind her story and asks for the whole truth (compare 1 Samuel 3:17).

decisions.choice: Ask me, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable puts the courtesy "Let my lord the king speak" as a plain invitation.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הֲיַ֥ד יוֹאָ֛ב אִתָּ֖ךְ בְּכָל־זֹ֑את וַתַּ֣עַן הָאִשָּׁ֣ה וַתֹּ֡אמֶר חֵֽי־נַפְשְׁךָ֩ אֲדֹנִ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אִם־אִ֣שׁ׀לְהֵמִ֣ין וּלְהַשְׂמִ֗יל מִכֹּ֤ל אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּֽי־עַבְדְּךָ֤ יוֹאָב֙ ה֣וּא צִוָּ֔נִי וְה֗וּא שָׂ֚ם בְּפִ֣י שִׁפְחָֽתְךָ֔ אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃
records.gloss: And said the king, [Is] the hand of Joab with you in all this? And answered the woman and said, [By the] life of your soul, my lord the king, if [there is one able] to turn right or to turn left from all that has spoken my lord the king; for your servant Joab, he commanded me, and he put in [the] mouth of your maidservant all the words the these.
pieces: The king asked, "Has Joab had a hand in all this with you?" The woman replied, "My lord the king, as surely as you live, no one can turn aside to the right or the left from anything my lord the king says. Yes, it was your servant Joab who gave me orders. He put all these words in your servant's mouth.

L.19: And the king said, "[Is] the hand of Joab with you in all this?" And the woman answered and said, "[As] your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from all that my lord the king has spoken; for your servant Joab, he commanded me, and he put all these words in the mouth of your maidservant.

R.19: The king asked, "Did Joab put you up to all this?" The woman answered, "Your Majesty, as surely as you live, no one can hide anything from you. Yes, it was your servant Joab who told me to do this. He told me everything I should say.

decisions.choice: is the hand of Joab with you: has Joab had a part in this
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for someone's doing or support (1 Samuel 22:17). The king guesses that Joab, who wanted Absalom back (verse 1), is behind her.

decisions.choice: no one can turn right or left from what my lord says: no one can get past the king
decisions.reason: To turn neither right nor left is to keep straight on a path (Deuteronomy 5:32). She means that no one can dodge the king's words; he has seen straight through to the truth. The word translated "there is" is an unusual spelling of the common word for "there is" (Micah 6:10).

decisions.choice: as your soul lives: an oath by the king's own life
decisions.reason: Swearing by the life of the person addressed was a solemn way to stress that one was speaking the truth (1 Samuel 1:26; 17:55).

decisions.choice: your servant Joab: a polite way of naming the king's officer
decisions.reason: Joab is called the king's servant, as courtesy required (verse 20). The woman also keeps calling herself "your maidservant" (verse 6).

decisions.choice: Did Joab put you up to all this?; no one can hide anything from you
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the two pictures, Joab's hand and turning right or left, mean.

records.source: לְבַעֲב֤וּר סַבֵּב֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י הַדָּבָ֔ר עָשָׂ֛ה עַבְדְּךָ֥ יוֹאָ֖ב אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַאדֹנִ֣י חָכָ֗ם כְּחָכְמַת֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים לָדַ֖עַת אֶֽת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּאָֽרֶץ׃ס
records.gloss: In order to turn around [the] face of the matter did your servant Joab the thing the this; and my lord [is] wise, like [the] wisdom of [the] angel of God, to know all that [is] in the land.
pieces: Your servant Joab did this to change the way things stand. But my lord is as wise as an angel of God, and knows everything that happens in the land."

L.20: In order to turn around the face of the matter, your servant Joab did this thing; but my lord [is] wise, like the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all that [is] on the earth."

R.20: He did this to change the way you see this matter. But Your Majesty, you are as wise as an angel from God. You know everything that happens in the land."

decisions.choice: to turn around the face of the matter: to change how things stand
decisions.reason: The "face" of a matter is how it looks and stands. Joab wanted to bring the affair of Absalom to a new turn by having the king see it in a new light, without asking openly himself.

decisions.choice: wise like the wisdom of an angel of God: wise beyond any ordinary person
decisions.reason: As in verse 17 and 1 Samuel 29:9. Here the praise is for wisdom: the king has seen through the story to Joab behind it.

decisions.choice: all that is in the land: everything that goes on
decisions.reason: The word can mean the land of Israel or the whole earth. In praise of a king it means that nothing that happens escapes him; the land he rules is likely meant.

decisions.choice: an angel of God (Literal, Balanced); an angel from God (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 17 and 1 Samuel 29:9.

decisions.choice: on the earth (Literal); in the land (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the wider sense of the word; Balanced and Readable say "in the land", following meaning decision m3.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֶל־יוֹאָ֔ב הִנֵּה־נָ֥א עָשִׂ֖יתִי אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וְלֵ֛ךְ הָשֵׁ֥ב אֶת־הַנַּ֖עַר אֶת־אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And said the king to Joab, Look please, I do the thing the this; and go, bring back the young man Absalom.
pieces: Then the king said to Joab, "Very well, I will do this. Go and bring back the young man Absalom."

L.21: And the king said to Joab, "Look now, I will do this thing. Go, bring back the young man Absalom."

R.21: Then the king said to Joab, "All right, I will do what you want. Go and bring young Absalom back."

decisions.choice: I will do: following the form the Hebrew tradition reads aloud
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "you have done this thing", while the traditional reading, followed here, is "I have done", meaning "I hereby grant" this. The written form would mean "You have accomplished this", that is, Joab has won his point. Either way the king agrees to Absalom's return.

decisions.choice: the young man Absalom: a word of tenderness as much as of age
decisions.reason: Absalom was a grown man with children of his own (verse 27). Calling him "the young man" may show the king's fondness for him, as in 18:5, where David asks the commanders to deal gently with the young man Absalom.

decisions.choice: Look now (Literal); Very well (Balanced); All right (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word that calls attention here marks the king's agreement.

records.heading: Absalom returns to Jerusalem

records.source: וַיִּפֹּל֩ יוֹאָ֨ב אֶל־פָּנָ֥יו אַ֛רְצָה וַיִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ וַיְבָ֣רֶךְ אֶת־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֡ב הַיּוֹם֩ יָדַ֨ע עַבְדְּךָ֜ כִּי־מָצָ֨אתִי חֵ֤ן בְּעֵינֶ֨יךָ֙ אֲדֹנִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֥ה הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And fell Joab on his face to [the] ground and bowed down and blessed the king. And said Joab, Today knows your servant that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, that has done the king the word of your servant.
pieces: Joab threw himself face down on the ground, bowed low and blessed the king. "Today," Joab said, "your servant knows that my lord the king looks on me with favor, because the king has granted your servant's request."

L.22: And Joab fell on his face to the ground and bowed down and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, in that the king has done the word of your servant."

R.22: Joab bowed down with his face to the ground. He thanked the king and asked God to bless him. He said, "Your Majesty, today I know that you are pleased with me, because you have done what I asked."

decisions.choice: blessed the king: thanked him and called down God's good on him
decisions.reason: To bless a superior is to thank him and to wish him God's blessing at the same time (19:40; 1 Samuel 25:32-33).

decisions.choice: found favor in your eyes: you look on me with kindness
decisions.reason: The phrase is used for being in good standing with a superior (Genesis 33:10; 1 Samuel 20:3).

decisions.choice: your servant: following the form the Hebrew tradition reads aloud
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "his servant"; the traditional reading, followed here, is "your servant". The sense is the same: Joab means himself.

decisions.choice: He thanked the king and asked God to bless him (Readable); looks on me with favor (Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable spells out both parts of "blessed" and uses "I" and "you" for the courtly third person, with "Your Majesty". Balanced says "my lord the king looks on me with favor" for "I have found favor in your eyes", following meaning decision m2.

records.source: וַיָּ֥קָם יוֹאָ֖ב וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ גְּשׁ֑וּרָה וַיָּבֵ֥א אֶת־אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃פ
records.gloss: And arose Joab and went to Geshur and brought Absalom [to] Jerusalem.
pieces: So Joab set out and went to Geshur, and he brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.

L.23: And Joab arose and went to Geshur, and he brought Absalom [to] Jerusalem.

R.23: So Joab got up and went to Geshur, and he brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: Geshur: a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee
decisions.reason: Absalom's mother Maacah was the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (3:3). Absalom fled to his grandfather there after Amnon's death and stayed three years (13:37-38).

decisions.choice: back to Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Jerusalem was Absalom's home before he fled, so Balanced and Readable say "back".

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ יִסֹּ֣ב אֶל־בֵּית֔וֹ וּפָנַ֖י לֹ֣א יִרְאֶ֑ה וַיִּסֹּ֤ב אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ אֶל־בֵּית֔וֹ וּפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֹ֥א רָאָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And said the king, Let him turn to his house, and my face not he will see. And turned Absalom to his house, and [the] face of the king not he saw.
pieces: But the king said, "He is to go to his own house. He must not come into my presence." So Absalom went to his own house and did not come into the king's presence.

L.24: And the king said, "Let him turn aside to his own house, and he shall not see my face." So Absalom turned aside to his own house, and he did not see the face of the king.

R.24: But the king said, "Absalom must go to his own house. I do not want to see him." So Absalom went to his own house, and he did not see the king.

decisions.choice: he shall not see my face: he is not to come before the king
decisions.reason: To see the king's face is to be received by him, to come into his presence at court (3:13; Genesis 43:3). Absalom may live in Jerusalem, but he is shut out from his father and from the court.

decisions.choice: the king's command repeated as what happened
decisions.reason: The second half of the verse repeats the king's words, now as fact, to stress that Absalom was home but still kept away. This sets up the two years of verse 28.

decisions.choice: come into my presence; come into the king's presence
decisions.reason: Balanced says what seeing the king's face means, following meaning decision m1. Readable keeps the plain words "see him" and "see the king".

records.source: וּכְאַבְשָׁל֗וֹם לֹא־הָיָ֧ה אִישׁ־יָפֶ֛ה בְּכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְהַלֵּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד מִכַּ֤ף רַגְלוֹ֙ וְעַ֣ד קָדְקֳד֔וֹ לֹא־הָ֥יָה ב֖וֹ מֽוּם׃
records.gloss: And like Absalom not was a man handsome in all Israel to praise greatly; from [the] sole of his foot and to the crown of his head not was in him a blemish.
pieces: In all Israel there was no man so highly praised for his good looks as Absalom; there was not a flaw in him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

L.25: And in all Israel there was no man as handsome as Absalom, to be praised greatly; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

R.25: No one in all Israel was as handsome as Absalom. Everyone praised how good he looked. From his feet to the top of his head, there was nothing wrong with the way he looked.

decisions.choice: from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head: his whole body
decisions.reason: The phrase takes in the whole person (Deuteronomy 28:35; Job 2:7). "Blemish" is the word used for a flaw that kept an animal from being offered or a priest from serving (Leviticus 21:17-23; 22:20). Absalom looked perfect.

decisions.choice: handsome, much praised: the looks that drew people to him
decisions.reason: Saul and David were also described as good-looking (1 Samuel 9:2; 16:12). Absalom's looks help explain how he later won the hearts of the people (15:6), and his hair, described next, plays a part in his death (18:9).

decisions.choice: Everyone praised how good he looked
decisions.reason: Readable makes the praise a sentence of its own.

records.source: וּֽבְגַלְּחוֹ֮ אֶת־רֹאשׁוֹ֒ וְֽ֠הָיָה מִקֵּ֨ץיָמִ֤ים׀לַיָּמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְגַלֵּ֔חַ כִּֽי־כָבֵ֥ד עָלָ֖יו וְגִלְּח֑וֹ וְשָׁקַל֙ אֶת־שְׂעַ֣ר רֹאשׁ֔וֹ מָאתַ֥יִם שְׁקָלִ֖ים בְּאֶ֥בֶן הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And when he shaved his head, and it was from [the] end of days to days that he shaved, for [it was] heavy on him and he shaved it, and he weighed [the] hair of his head, two hundred shekels by [the] stone of the king.
pieces: Whenever he cut his hair, which he did once a year because it grew heavy on him, he would weigh it, and it came to {{units:about 5 pounds by the royal standard|200 shekels by the king's weight}}.

L.26: And when he cut the hair of his head, and it was at the end of every year that he cut [it], because it was heavy on him, so he cut it, he weighed the hair of his head: 200 shekels by the king's weight.

R.26: Once a year Absalom cut his hair, because it became too heavy for him. When he weighed the hair he had cut off, it came to {{units:about 5 pounds by the royal standard|200 shekels by the king's weight}}.

decisions.choice: from the end of days to days: once a year
decisions.reason: "Days" can mean a year, as in the yearly sacrifice (1 Samuel 1:3, 21; 20:6). The verse says how often he cut his hair, not that he cut it at any particular season.

decisions.choice: 200 shekels by the king's weight: about 5 pounds
decisions.reason: The shekel was a weight, about 2/5 of an ounce. "The king's weight" was a royal standard used to check weights, set beside the standard of the sanctuary (Exodus 30:13). The figure shows how thick his hair was; some think the number has grown in copying, but the text gives no other figure.

decisions.choice: shaved: cut his hair
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to shave close or simply to cut the hair. Here it means a yearly haircut, since his hair grew back heavy each year.

decisions.choice: about 5 pounds by the royal standard (default); 200 shekels by the king's weight (alternative)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight first, with the original unit as the alternative, as for other weights; Literal keeps the shekel.

decisions.choice: the parenthesis
decisions.reason: The Hebrew breaks off to say how often and why he cut his hair, then picks up its sentence again. Literal keeps the broken sentence with commas; Balanced turns the aside into a clause beginning "which"; Readable puts the facts in order.

records.source: וַיִּֽוָּלְד֤וּ לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ שְׁלוֹשָׁ֣ה בָנִ֔ים וּבַ֥ת אַחַ֖ת וּשְׁמָ֣הּ תָּמָ֑ר הִ֣יא הָיְתָ֔ה אִשָּׁ֖ה יְפַ֥ת מַרְאֶֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And were born to Absalom three sons and daughter one, and her name [was] Tamar; she was a woman beautiful of appearance.
pieces: Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. His daughter's name was Tamar, and she was a beautiful woman.

L.27: And to Absalom were born three sons and one daughter, and her name [was] Tamar; she was a woman beautiful of appearance.

R.27: Absalom had three sons and one daughter. His daughter's name was Tamar, and she was very beautiful.

decisions.choice: Tamar: named after Absalom's sister
decisions.reason: Absalom's sister Tamar, as beautiful as this daughter, was raped by Amnon (13:1, 14). Absalom seems to have named his daughter after her.

decisions.choice: three sons: sons who seem to have died young
decisions.reason: In 18:18 Absalom says that he has no son to keep his name alive, so these sons apparently did not survive. The text does not explain this. The ancient Greek translation adds that Tamar became the wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijah, which the Hebrew does not have (compare 1 Kings 15:2, where Abijam's mother is Maacah, Absalom's daughter or granddaughter).

decisions.choice: a beautiful woman (Balanced); very beautiful (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Beautiful of appearance" is said in plain English.

records.source: וַיֵּ֧שֶׁב אַבְשָׁל֛וֹם בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם שְׁנָתַ֣יִם יָמִ֑ים וּפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֹ֥א רָאָֽה׃
records.gloss: And dwelt Absalom in Jerusalem two years [of] days, and [the] face of the king not he saw.
pieces: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without coming into the king's presence.

L.28: And Absalom lived in Jerusalem two full years, and he did not see the face of the king.

R.28: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two whole years, and in all that time he never saw the king.

decisions.choice: two years of days: two full years
decisions.reason: "Days" added to a length of time means it was complete (Genesis 41:1). Two years passed, after three in Geshur (13:38), and Absalom was still kept from his father.

decisions.choice: without coming into the king's presence
decisions.reason: As in verse 24.

records.heading: Absalom sees the king again

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח אַבְשָׁל֜וֹם אֶל־יוֹאָ֗ב לִשְׁלֹ֤חַ אֹתוֹ֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְלֹ֥א אָבָ֖ה לָב֣וֹא אֵלָ֑יו וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח עוֹד֙ שֵׁנִ֔ית וְלֹ֥א אָבָ֖ה לָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: And sent Absalom to Joab to send him to the king, and not he was willing to come to him; and he sent again a second [time], and not he was willing to come.
pieces: Absalom then sent for Joab, meaning to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent a second time, but still Joab would not come.

L.29: And Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he was not willing to come to him. And he sent again a second time, but he was not willing to come.

R.29: Then Absalom sent for Joab, because he wanted Joab to go to the king for him. But Joab refused to come. Absalom sent for him a second time, but Joab still would not come.

decisions.choice: to send him to the king: to have Joab go to the king for him
decisions.reason: Absalom wants Joab to plead for him again, as he did through the woman of Tekoa. Joab, who had arranged his return, now keeps away, perhaps not wanting to risk the king's displeasure a second time.

decisions.choice: Joab would not come
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he was not willing". Balanced and Readable name Joab, so that it is clear who refused.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֶל־עֲבָדָ֜יו רְאוּ֩ חֶלְקַ֨ת יוֹאָ֤ב אֶל־יָדִי֙ וְלוֹ־שָׁ֣ם שְׂעֹרִ֔ים לְכ֖וּ וְהַצִּית֣וּהָ בָאֵ֑שׁ וַיַּצִּ֜תוּ עַבְדֵ֧י אַבְשָׁל֛וֹם אֶת־הַחֶלְקָ֖ה בָּאֵֽשׁ׃פ
records.gloss: And he said to his servants, See, [the] portion of Joab [is] next to my hand, and he has there barley; go and set it on fire with fire. And set on fire [the] servants of Absalom the portion with fire.
pieces: So he told his servants, "You see Joab's field beside mine, where he has barley growing. Go and set fire to it." And Absalom's servants set fire to the field.

L.30: And he said to his slaves, "See, Joab's field [is] next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire." So the slaves of Absalom set the field on fire.

R.30: So Absalom said to his servants, "Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley growing there. Go and burn it." So Absalom's servants set fire to the field.

decisions.choice: next to my hand: beside my land
decisions.reason: "Hand" here means side or place, so the field lies next to Absalom's own.

decisions.choice: burning the barley: destroying a year's harvest
decisions.reason: Barley was ripe in early spring. Burning a field ready for harvest was a serious loss and an act of war (compare Samson in Judges 15:4-5). Absalom uses it to force Joab to come to him.

decisions.choice: go and set it on fire: following the form the Hebrew tradition reads aloud
alternatives: and I will set it on fire
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has a form that can be read "and I will set it on fire"; the traditional reading, followed here, is the command "and set it on fire". The ancient Greek translation adds that Joab's servants came to him with torn clothes and told him what had happened; the Hebrew does not have this.

decisions.choice: field; set it on fire (Literal); set fire to it (Balanced); burn it (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Portion" of land is a field, and "set on fire with fire" is said once, as English does.

decisions.choice: his servants: members of Absalom's household who belonged to him
decisions.reason: The word is the one for a slave or servant owned by a master, not hired. A king's son kept a large household of them (13:28-29, where his young men carry out his order to kill Amnon).

decisions.choice: slaves (Literal); servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As the style of this translation sets out, Literal keeps "slaves" and Balanced and Readable say "servants", while meaning decision m4 keeps the sense of the word.

records.source: וַיָּ֣קָם יוֹאָ֔ב וַיָּבֹ֥א אֶל־אַבְשָׁל֖וֹם הַבָּ֑יְתָה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֔יו לָ֣מָּה הִצִּ֧יתוּ עֲבָדֶ֛ךָ אֶת־הַחֶלְקָ֥ה אֲשֶׁר־לִ֖י בָּאֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And arose Joab and came to Absalom to the house, and said to him, Why have set on fire your servants the portion which [is] mine with fire?
pieces: Then Joab went straight to Absalom at his house and said, "Why did your servants set fire to my field?"

L.31: And Joab arose and came to Absalom at [his] house, and said to him, "Why have your slaves set my field on fire?"

R.31: Then Joab went to Absalom's house and asked him, "Why did your servants burn my field?"

decisions.choice: arose and came: Joab came at once
decisions.reason: The burning worked. Joab, who would not come when sent for, now comes to Absalom's house himself. Balanced says he went "straight" there to bring out the haste of "arose and came".

decisions.choice: [his] house
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the house"; Absalom's house is meant.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אַבְשָׁל֣וֹם אֶל־יוֹאָ֡ב הִנֵּ֣ה שָׁלַ֣חְתִּי אֵלֶ֣יךָ׀לֵאמֹ֡ר בֹּ֣א הֵ֠נָּה וְאֶשְׁלְחָה֩ אֹתְךָ֨אֶל־הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לֵאמֹ֗ר לָ֤מָּה בָּ֨אתִי֙ מִגְּשׁ֔וּר ט֥וֹב לִ֖י עֹ֣ד אֲנִי־שָׁ֑ם וְעַתָּ֗ה אֶרְאֶה֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְאִם־יֶשׁ־בִּ֥י עָוֺ֖ן וֶהֱמִתָֽנִי׃
records.gloss: And said Absalom to Joab, Look, I sent to you, saying, Come here, and I will send you to the king to say, Why have I come from Geshur? [It would be] good for me [if] still I [were] there. And now let me see [the] face of the king; and if there is in me iniquity, let him kill me.
pieces: Absalom answered Joab, "I sent word to you to come here, so that I could send you to the king to ask, 'Why did I come back from Geshur? I would be better off if I were still there.' Now let me come into the king's presence. If I am guilty of anything, let him put me to death."

L.32: And Absalom said to Joab, "Look, I sent to you, saying, 'Come here, so that I may send you to the king to say, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me [if] I [were] still there."' And now let me see the face of the king, and if there is iniquity in me, let him put me to death."

R.32: Absalom answered Joab, "I sent for you because I wanted you to go to the king for me. I wanted you to ask him, 'Why did I come back from Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there.' Now I want to see the king. If I have done something wrong, let him kill me."

decisions.choice: why have I come from Geshur: it would have been better to stay in exile
decisions.reason: Absalom's question is a complaint. To be back in Jerusalem but shut out from the king is worse to him than exile, where he lived as a prince at his grandfather's court (13:37).

decisions.choice: if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me: let the king judge me openly
decisions.reason: Absalom demands to be either received or condemned. The word for "iniquity" is the guilt of wrongdoing (verse 9). He treats the killing of Amnon as a question the king has never settled.

decisions.choice: see the face of the king: be received by the king
decisions.reason: As in verses 24 and 28.

decisions.choice: quotes inside quotes
decisions.reason: Absalom quotes his own message, which in turn quotes what Joab was to say. Literal shows each step with its own quotation marks; Balanced and Readable shorten the first step to plain report.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֨א יוֹאָ֣ב אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ֮ וַיַּגֶּד־לוֹ֒ וַיִּקְרָ֤א אֶל־אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ וַיָּבֹ֣א אֶל־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיִּשְׁתַּ֨חוּ ל֧וֹ עַל־אַפָּ֛יו אַ֖רְצָה לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיִּשַּׁ֥ק הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לְאַבְשָׁלֽוֹם׃פ
records.gloss: And came Joab to the king and told him; and he called Absalom, and he came to the king and bowed down to him on his face to [the] ground before the king, and kissed the king Absalom.
pieces: So Joab went to the king and told him, and the king summoned Absalom. Absalom came to the king and bowed down before him with his face to the ground, and the king kissed Absalom.

L.33: And Joab came to the king and told him, and he called Absalom. And he came to the king and bowed down to him on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.

R.33: So Joab went to the king and told him what Absalom had said. Then the king sent for Absalom. Absalom came in and bowed down in front of the king with his face to the ground. And the king kissed him.

decisions.choice: bowed down and was kissed: Absalom submits, and the king receives him
decisions.reason: Absalom bows as a subject before his king; the king's kiss is a sign that he is received back into favor and into the family (compare Genesis 33:4; 45:15). The story does not say whether father and son were truly reconciled, and the next chapter tells of Absalom's revolt.

decisions.choice: told him ... called: the king summoned Absalom
decisions.reason: The one who calls Absalom is the king, after hearing Joab's report.

decisions.choice: the king summoned (Balanced); the king sent for (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the king as the one who called, which the Hebrew leaves to the context. Readable adds "what Absalom had said" to say what Joab told him.
